systems make end-to-end research automation increasingly plausible, but they target relatively
stable scientific domains. We argue that AI-native cybersecurity is a different kind of scientific

pipeline. The pipeline begins with agenda setting—strategic questions, scenario definitions, and
governance constraints—and then moves through problem framing, literature and threat analysis,
toolsmithing, controlled execution, evaluation, and scientific reporting. Across this flow sits a
role layer of specialized agents: problem-framing agents, literature agents, threat-modeling agents,
toolsmithing agents, experiment managers, evaluators, and reporting agents. These agents do not
operate as free-form generalists. They invoke bounded procedures that encode reusable capabilities
and stable interaction patterns.

evidence.excerpt:
Several challenges remain open. Defense targets are heterogeneous: what works for one class of
organizational system, critical infrastructure asset, or digital platform may fail for another, and
broad-transfer claims will require much stronger empirical programs than a framework paper can
supply. The dual-use problem is intrinsic rather than peripheral: many capabilities required for
high-quality security research are also offensively repurposable, which is why containment, release
control, auditability, and permission design are central rather than ornamental. The experimental
substrate is unusually demanding: cybersecurity research often needs digital twins, replayable
environments, sandboxing, and high-integrity evidence capture, and poorly designed environments
can produce misleading conclusions even when nominal benchmark outcomes look strong.

single organizational realization. One practical realization is a modular multi-agent
research system built around bounded capability packages, explicit tools, controlled environments,
and continuous calibration. Across the four axes, representative agendas—from hidden-defect
discovery at frontier capability, through calibrated assistance and multi-model routing, to resilient
agent legions and the deconstruction of terminal security into agent security, and on to strategic

of this paper is to fix the category, the design pressures, and an initial architecture on which later
systems, benchmarks, and empirical programs can be built.

primary.claim_evidence_alignment: The conceptual definitions, taxonomy, and architectural descriptions are internally consistent with the authors' framing, but the manuscript explicitly acknowledges that broad empirical validation remains an open agenda.
primary.evaluation_assessment: There is no empirical evaluation, experimental testing, or benchmark validation of the proposed system architecture. The paper discusses existing external systems and studies conceptually rather than assessing an operational prototype of Hephaestus.

evaluation_independence.final_evaluation_signal: Not applicable; no experimental or benchmark evaluation was conducted.
evaluation_independence.optimization_signal: Not applicable; no models or systems were trained, tuned, or algorithmically optimized in this conceptual framework paper.

primary.limitations: The authors explicitly note that the framework lacks empirical realization, that heterogeneous defense targets make general transfer unverified, and that institutional placement remains open.
primary.method_assessment: The methodology is entirely conceptual and architectural, synthesizing related work to propose layered roles (framing, toolsmithing, execution, evaluation, governance) and design requirements for autonomous cybersecurity research without formal algorithmic specifications or an implemented codebase.
primary.quality_rationale: While the framework provides thoughtful conceptual framing and literature synthesis for autonomous cybersecurity research, it contains no implemented prototype, empirical experiments, or formal evaluation, creating scientific uncertainty regarding its practical feasibility and effectiveness.
primary.scoped_contribution: The manuscript presents a conceptual and architectural framework defining the 'Cybersecurity AI Scientist' as an adversarial, event-driven research object, structured around a 'four-zeros' objective frame and a modular multi-agent pipeline.

scholarly_quality.rationale: While the framework provides thoughtful conceptual framing and literature synthesis for autonomous cybersecurity research, it contains no implemented prototype, empirical experiments, or formal evaluation, creating scientific uncertainty regarding its practical feasibility and effectiveness.
scholarly_quality.uncertainty: The authors explicitly note that the framework lacks empirical realization, that heterogeneous defense targets make general transfer unverified, and that institutional placement remains open.
